newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU plans further meetings with U.S. on internet trade.
newsitem.headline: EU plans further meetings with U.S. on internet trade.

text.p: The European Commission is seeking further meetings with U.S. trade officials to try to settle differences on how to prepare for an expected boom in internet trade before the end of the century.

European Commission officials said, however, that while differences remained between Washington and Brussels over some aspects of internet trade, there was broad agreement that the internet should be as unregulated as possible.
"We have much more agreement than disagreement," a Commission official said. "We feel we have the basis of something we can work with and need to meet again to take it further."
The official was speaking following a key conference in Bonn earlier this week where the Commission and U.S. outlined their ideas for commercial trade on the internet.
Ira Magaziner, the U.S. envoy appointed by President Clinton to take charge of internet trade, also passed through Brussels on Thursday for further meetings with Commission officials on the subject.

The chief area of disagreement between the EU and U.S. centres on so-called "data protection" whereby customers buying goods or services over the internet are guaranteed their personal details are kept secret.
The EU is currently drafting laws to make it illegal for traders to pass on customer details obtained on the internet to other suppliers, but the U.S. says this should be a self-regulatory exercise.

The trade in mailing lists of electronic addresses is already a huge business in the U.S. with thousands of companies selling goods ranging from weight-loss programmes to holidays bombarding hundreds of thousands of internet users with unsolicited "E-mail".
European users of U.S internet service providers such as Compuserve and America Online are already receiving dozens of junk E-mails a week, but European service providers have largely resisted this.

During this week's Bonn meeting ministers from 40 countries agreed that Internet regulations should be led by private enterprise rather than governments, but also wrestled with thorny issues such as taxation on goods or services bought on the electronic network.
The ministers vowed to make a joint effort to clamp down on tax evasion on business deals conducted on the Internet.
